newsitem.title: USA: Clinton may speak out on Republican tax plans.
newsitem.headline: Clinton may speak out on Republican tax plans.

text.p: President Clinton may speak out this week, possibly Tuesday, to drive home the point that Republican tax cut bills as currently drafted are not acceptable to him, administration officials said Monday.
The officials, who asked not to be named, said the White House was waiting to see how talks went Monday before deciding whether Clinton would go public with the criticism.
"The overriding dynamic here is the fact that there's been very little, if any, movement towards the administration," said one official. "We're not making much progress at the moment."
Negotiators from the House and Senate met with administration officials throughout the weekend to discuss their rival plans to cut taxes by $85 billion over the next five years.

Those plans flesh out the balanced-budget accord Clinton reached with the Republicans who control Congress in May. That pact, reached after months of negotiations, aims to eliminate the federal budget deficit by 2002 while cutting taxes.
Congressional negotiators have said that they would like to complete the legislation needed to enact that agreement by their August recess, scheduled to begin in two weeks.

"We'd like to get this done and we'd like to sign a bill, but the president's not going to sign a bad bill," said one administration official. "If that's not abundantly clear, we're going to make it (clear) this week."

The officials said that if Clinton speaks out, his remarks would essentially restate points he made in a letter sent over the weekend to the Republican chairmen of the congressional tax-writing committees and their ranking Democratic members.
In that letter, he argued that neither of the tax bills passed by the House and Senate "provides an adequate share of tax relief to middle-income families."
It also said that both plans "failed a critical test of fairness" by denying the benefits of a proposed $500 per child tax credit to families that earn less than $30,000 per year.
While Clinton disagrees with parts of both the House and the Senate bills, the Senate version appears more palatable to him than the House draft.
Administration officials said Senate negotiators seemed to be moving closer to the House version -- with the result that, as one official put it, they are moving "further away from us."
